analysis.one_liner: Fully repeals the Affordable Care Act and restores the pre-2010 health care and student loan laws.
analysis.headline: Sole sponsor, zero cosponsors: the full Obamacare repeal bill sat in eight House committees without a hearing or a vote and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have wiped the Affordable Care Act off the books entirely, effective October 1, 2023, along with the companion 2010 law that finished the health law and rewrote student loans. Every rule created by those laws — protections for people with preexisting conditions, Medicaid expansion, tax credits that help people buy insurance, the taxes on high earners that pay for them — would be undone, and the law as it stood before 2010 restored. It got no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the clearest financial winners would be high-income households: the ACA's taxes fall on upper incomes, including a surtax on investment income and an added Medicare payroll tax for top earners. Health insurers would also be freed from rules like guaranteed issue, required coverage levels, and limits on how much premium money goes to patient care rather than profit and administration.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals both the Affordable Care Act and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, effective October 1, 2023.

Every provision of law that those acts amended or repealed would be restored as if they had never been enacted, unwinding ACA taxes, market rules, Medicaid expansion, and the 2010 law's changes to student loans.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on people who depend on the ACA: those with preexisting conditions who could be denied or priced out of coverage, millions of Marketplace and Medicaid-expansion enrollees, young adults insured through a parent's plan, seniors who benefit from closed prescription drug coverage gaps and free preventive care, and students who benefited from the 2010 law's changes to student loans.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with preexisting conditions and ACA enrollees

drawbacks.text: Repeal would restore the pre-2010 legal landscape in which insurers could deny coverage or charge more for preexisting conditions, ending protections that tens of millions of Americans now rely on.

A good-faith supporter would acknowledge the real costs imposed by the ACA that repeal addresses: taxes concentrated on high earners and investment income, and higher premiums for some middle-class buyers who earn too much for subsidies.
The bill offered no replacement plan — no alternative for the subsidies, protections, or Medicaid expansion it eliminated — which is why it drew no cosponsors even among Republicans.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax relief and regulatory freedom for high earners and insurers are real, but they come at the price of stripping coverage and protections from millions of people with nothing offered in exchange. The bill's own momentum — zero cosponsors in a chamber where Republicans held a majority — reflects that the costs overwhelmingly outweigh the gains.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to eight committees, sat through two subcommittee referrals, never got a hearing or a floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs introduced the bill on January 9, 2023, the first week of the 118th Congress.

It was referred to eight House committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Natural Resources, Judiciary, House Administration, Rules, and Appropriations — and to subcommittees, where it stalled without action.
No member joined as a cosponsor over the bill's two-year lifespan.
The bill never received a hearing or a vote in any committee or on the House floor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The outcome preserved the Affordable Care Act's protections and subsidies for the tens of millions of people who rely on them; no one had to defeat the bill — it simply went nowhere.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyone who kept ACA coverage and protections

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the full-repeal bill on January 9, 2023; it received no cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was strictly a one-man effort: a Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party, and no vote ever took place.

industries.note: Repeal would free insurers from guaranteed issue, essential benefits, and medical loss ratio rules — but it would also cut them off from the federal tax credits that bring millions of paying customers to the marketplace. Their freedom would come directly at the cost of protections and subsidies their customers rely on.

The ACA's financing falls on upper incomes — an investment income surtax and an added Medicare payroll tax for top earners. Repeal is effectively a large tax cut for the wealthiest households, paid for by ending subsidies and protections for ordinary buyers.
